title: Running PostgreSQL from a single executable
excerpt: minipg bundles PostgreSQL in a .pgdb directory and starts a server only when needed.
body:
A 35 MB download is all that separates a fully-featured PostgreSQL instance from a blank browser tab. The minipg demo page pulls that single file, boots the PostgreSQL binaries inside Docker Hub’s `postgres:18-alpine` image, and immediately offers a `psql` prompt with `minipg app.pgdb`. No Docker daemon, no virtual machine, and no separate Linux kernel are required; the h9 runtime emulates the needed kernel calls directly on the host hypervisor.

The demo runs the Linux build of minipg inside the Postgres image, starts the server on a Unix socket (a page cannot open a TCP port), and hands the client tools over to the same h9 instance. Because the image already contains the PostgreSQL executables and the h9 runtime, the whole stack launches in the browser with a single network request.

In the sections that follow you will see how minipg packages PostgreSQL, how it runs commands without a permanent server, how it fits into CI pipelines, and what the performance trade-offs look like.

## How minipg packages PostgreSQL

minipg bundles Docker Hub’s `postgres:18-alpine` image and runs it with the h9 runtime. h9 provides a Plan 9-style kernel that answers Linux system calls, so the Alpine PostgreSQL binaries execute directly on the host hypervisor. There is no separate Linux kernel to boot, no VM image to manage, and no Docker process lingering in the background.

All data for a database lives in a single `.pgdb` directory. Inside that folder you will find `minipg.toml` (settings and the generated super-user password) and `pgdata/`, PostgreSQL’s data directory stored as plain files.

Because everything is self-contained, the directory can be copied, archived, or moved like any other folder. New clusters are created from a template baked into the minipg build; the template avoids the half-minute `initdb` step that a regular Docker container would need, making the first start almost instantaneous.

A concrete example of creating a database and opening a shell looks like this:

```bash
minipg app.pgdb          # creates app.pgdb if missing and drops you into psql
minipg app.pgdb "select 1"   # runs a single statement and exits
minipg serve app.pgdb         # foreground server that stays up until stopped
minipg dump app.pgdb > dump.sql
minipg restore app.pgdb < dump.sql
```

## Running commands without a persistent server

When a minipg command is invoked, the tool checks whether a PostgreSQL process is already running for the target `.pgdb`. If not, it launches a short-lived h9 machine, starts the server in the background, runs the requested client tool (`psql`, `pg_dump`, etc.), and shuts the server down once it becomes idle. Exactly one server process can exist per `.pgdb`; a lock file enforces this invariant.

Each client runs in its own h9 instance, which starts in roughly 90 ms. That overhead is small enough that occasional commands feel like native tools. The workflow is deliberately stateless: commands never host PostgreSQL themselves, they merely ask the existing server (or a freshly spawned one) to do the work.

Because the server stops automatically when idle, there is no need to remember a manual shutdown, and the lock prevents two processes from stepping on each other, keeping the data directory safe from corruption.

## Using minipg in CI pipelines

The Linux binary that minipg ships is statically linked and needs no privileged devices such as `/dev/kvm`. A continuous-integration job can be as short as:

```bash
minipg init test.pgdb
minipg run test.pgdb -- go test ./...
```

The `init` command creates the `.pgdb` directory and writes the initial configuration. The subsequent `run` command starts the server only for the duration of the test suite, then lets it shut down automatically. Because the server is transient, the CI runner does not need to manage a long-running PostgreSQL service, and the `.pgdb` directory can be cached between steps or copied to another runner without special handling.

Documentation on the project site lists every command, and the full manual is available on the same page. The source lives on GitHub under the MIT license, so inspection or forking is straightforward.

## Building minipg from source

If compiling a personal copy is preferred, the process is straightforward:

```bash
git clone --recursive https://github.com/progrium/minipg
cd minipg
make build          # pulls the root for the host architecture and builds ./minipg
make root ARCH=386  # optional: build a 386-bit root image
make web            # builds the demo page into .zig-out/web
```

The build requires Zig 0.16, plus `curl`, `jq`, `tar`, and `xz` for extracting the root image. The resulting `./minipg` binary can be dropped onto any Linux host that matches the architecture and will run without additional dependencies.

## Performance and reliability caveats

The project is still early, and h9’s Linux personality is young. On h9’s native backend, PostgreSQL runs about twice as slow as a native installation for a single client, and the slowdown grows under load. The source explicitly warns not to trust minipg with data that cannot be recreated. In practice this means using it for development, testing, or CI where the database can be regenerated, but avoiding it for production workloads that require high throughput or strict durability guarantees.

If bugs appear or questions arise, the authors ask that issues be filed on the GitHub repository rather than opened in a separate forum.

## The takeaway

minipg turns PostgreSQL into a single executable that stores everything in a portable `.pgdb` directory and spins up a server only when a command needs one. That model eliminates Docker, VMs, and permanent services, making it a tidy fit for lightweight development and CI environments. The trade-off is a noticeable performance penalty, about 2× slower on h9’s native backend, and reduced reliability under load, so it should stay out of production pipelines that handle irreplaceable data.
